title: Garifoto
author: Selassie Atadika
desc: A chef's boarding-school dish — gari dampened with salted water until damp but not soaking wet, then folded through a tomato stew off the heat.
longDesc: Garifoto is gari turned into a meal, and this version comes from a Ghanaian chef who frames it as made with the provisions boarding-school pupils typically took with them, a comforting dish for difficult times. A quarter teaspoon of salt is dissolved in half a cup of water and sprinkled over a cup and a half of gari until it is damp but not soaking wet. Carrots, green beans and green pepper are blanched. Onion, garlic, ginger, tomatoes, prekese and chilli cook until the stew is developed, the vegetables go in for five minutes, then the heat drops and the gari is folded through.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups gari (dried grated cassava) — or cooked couscous or fonio
1/4 tsp salt, plus more for blanching
1/2 cup water, for dampening the gari
4 tbsp palm oil, or olive oil
1 tsp dried mushroom, fish or shrimp powder (optional)
2 tsp minced chilli, or to taste
steps: Dissolve the 1/4 teaspoon of salt in 1/2 cup of water and add it to the gari until it is damp but not soaking wet.
Blanch the carrots, green beans and green pepper in salted water.
Sauté the onion in the palm and vegetable oils until softened.
Add the garlic, ginger, tomatoes, powder if using, chilli, salt and prekese, and cook until the stew is developed.
Add the blanched vegetables and cook approximately 5 minutes.
Mix in the moistened gari until it is damp but not soaked — it will continue to absorb the sauce.
Serve about one cup of garifoto per portion, topped with the basil ribbons and an egg.
chefTips: Damp but not soaking wet, twice — once when you dampen the gari and again when you fold it through. Her phrase, and it is the whole technique: gari keeps absorbing, so stop before it looks right.
It will continue to absorb the sauce after the heat is off. That is why you turn the heat off rather than cooking it on.
Half a cup of salted water to a cup and a half of gari for the initial dampening. Precise, and worth measuring.
Blanch the vegetables separately. They keep their colour and bite rather than going soft in the stew.
Prekese is the Ghanaian aromatic — Tetrapleura tetraptera, the four-winged fruit. She offers allspice as the substitute, which is not the same but is in the right direction.
Couscous or fonio will stand in for gari, by her own note. Fonio in particular behaves similarly.
Basil ribbons and an egg on top are not a garnish — they are what turns it from a side into a meal.
commonMistakes: Over-wetting the gari at either stage.
Cooking it on after the gari goes in.
Boiling the vegetables in the stew.
Using plain nutmeg or no aromatic in place of prekese.
sources: Adapted from 'Cooking in Quarantine: A Ghanaian chef's go-to Garifoto', Al Jazeera, published 19 April 2020. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'By Selassie Atadika', with the credit line 'Recipe courtesy of Selassie Atadika'. Atadika is the Ghanaian chef behind Midunu in Accra. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

A TRANSPARENCY NOTE ON SOURCING: the second fetch of this page came from a mirror host rather than aljazeera.com. The mirror appeared as a search result and the quantities matched the primary page exactly, so the figures are treated as TWO-PASS across two hosts — but the fact that one pass was not from the publisher's own domain is recorded rather than glossed over.

YIELD: not stated on the primary page. The fetch summaries said 'approximately 4', WHICH IS A SUMMARISER INFERENCE AND UNVERIFIED. The four servings above rests on the four eggs and the one-cup-per-portion serving note, and is editorial.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1½ cups gari (dried grated cassava) – can be substituted with cooked couscous or fonio; ¼ tsp salt, plus more for blanching; 60g carrots, medium dice; 60g green beans, medium dice; 60g green pepper, medium dice; 6 Tbsp vegetable oil; 4 Tbsp palm oil (or olive oil); 125g onion, medium dice; 1tsp garlic, minced; 2tsp fresh ginger, grated; 340g tomatoes, seeded and diced; 1tsp dried mushroom, fish or shrimp powder (optional); ½tsp prekese (Tetrapleura tetraptera, allspice, or your favourite spice blend); 2tsp (or to taste) minced chilli; 8 basil leaves, cut into ribbons; 4 eggs, cooked as desired.

A LIST OMISSION, flagged: the ½ cup of water for dampening the gari and the salted blanching water are BOTH IN THE METHOD BUT NOT IN THE INGREDIENT LIST. They are carried in the list above because without them the recipe cannot be followed.

Method as printed: dissolve ¼ tsp salt in ½ cup water and sprinkle over the gari 'until it is damp but not soaking wet'; blanch the vegetables; sauté onions in palm and vegetable oil; add garlic, ginger, tomatoes, powder, chilli, salt and prekese 'and cook until the stew is developed'; add the blanched vegetables and cook about 5 minutes; reduce to low and mix in the gari 'until the gari is damp but not soaked ... will continue to absorb the sauce'; serve 1 cup per dish with basil and eggs on top.

THE DONENESS CUES, both quoted: 'until the stew is developed' for the sauce, and 'damp but not soaking wet' / 'damp but not soaked ... will continue to absorb the sauce' for the gari. The second is the one that matters.
HEADNOTE, verbatim, and the reason the cultural note reads as it does: 'Made with provisions Ghanaian boarding school pupils typically took with them, a comforting dish for difficult times.'
FERMENTATION: none. Gari is a bought ingredient here, not prepared — its own production is a fermentation and is not published in this collection.

A SECOND DOCUMENTED VERSION, published separately at GHA056: Fran Osseo-Asare's 'Recipe #3: Pot Luck Gari foto'. The two differ substantially — this one is vegetable-led and vegetarian, hers is built on corned beef — and neither is corrected toward the other.
A NAMING NOTE: Osseo-Asare records elsewhere that gari foto is sometimes called 'gari jollof' in Ghana, which is why that name appears in the local-name field.
Whitby 1968, the CSIR bulletin, mentions gari foto only in passing — 'dried fish and egg' — and not as a recipe entry.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. The gari continues to absorb and firms up.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of water, or eat at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Gari is gluten-free and supplies resistant starch.
A generous blanched-vegetable load keeps most of its vitamin C.
Eggs make it a complete protein.
Red palm oil contributes provitamin-A carotenoids.
culturalNote: Gari keeps without refrigeration, which is why it went to boarding school in a tin and why garifoto exists at all — a hot meal from dry store cupboard goods. That one of Ghana's best-known chefs published it during a lockdown, framed as comfort food for difficult times, is a neat closing of that circle.
